Concepts Whisper While Syntax Shouts:
Spectral Anti-Concentration and the Dual Geometry
of Transformer Representations

Pratyush Acharya ††thanks: Correspondence to: acharya.pratyush@gmail.com    Nuraj Rimal    Habish Dhakal
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We test whether the causal inner product of Park et al. [2024]—defined by the unembedding covariance Σ\Sigma—enables cross-lingual concept transport. Across 17 models and 4 language pairs, a matched-spectrum randomization test finds that Whitened Causal Alignment is indistinguishable from spectral regularization alone (p=0.95p=0.95). However, this failure reveals a broader phenomenon: anti-concentration is observed in residual-stream difference-of-means vectors across five architecture families (p<10−33p<10^{-33}) and supported by SAE features (e.g., p=4.5×10−19p=4.5\times 10^{-19}) and linear probes on Gemma and Llama. We discover a dual geometry: activation-space concept directions anti-concentrate in the spectral tail, while static unembedding-row contrasts concentrate in high-variance directions (p<10−4p<10^{-4}). Split-injection causal interventions support the functional basis on Gemma and Llama (Cohen’s dd up to 1.801.80), and POS-tag probing across 8 models shows syntax preferentially encodes in the high-variance subspace in 6 of 8 architectures (p<0.013p<0.013), with the Qwen 2.5 family showing a significant reversal consistent with architecture-specific spectral structure. These results suggest transformers may rotate semantic content into spectrally quiet regions during contextualized processing, encoding concepts where they can be manipulated with reduced grammatical disruption.

1 Introduction

The mechanistic interpretability of large language models (LLMs) rests on a foundational empirical observation: high-level concepts appear to be encoded as linear directions in the model’s activation space [Mikolov et al., 2013a, Mikolov et al., 2013b, Marks and Tegmark, 2024, Tigges et al., 2024, Nanda et al., 2023]. This Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH) has been formalized by Park et al. [2024], who demonstrate that the appropriate geometric structure for these representations is not the standard Euclidean inner product, but rather a causal inner product defined by the inverse covariance of the unembedding matrix. Under this metric, causally separable concepts are provably orthogonal [Park et al., 2024, Park et al., 2025].

Simultaneously, the Platonic Representation Hypothesis [Huh et al., 2024] and related work on universal feature spaces [Lan et al., 2024] suggest that sufficiently capable models converge toward shared internal representations, raising the possibility of cross-lingual concept transport: extracting a concept direction from one language’s representation and injecting it into another’s via Procrustes alignment [Conneau et al., 2018, Conneau et al., 2020].

The intersection of these two hypotheses—that concepts live in a specific causal geometry, and that this geometry is shared across languages—motivates what we term Whitened Causal Alignment (wca): aligning representation spaces after whitening with the inverse square root of their respective unembedding covariance matrices. If the causal geometry hypothesis is correct, wca should outperform naive Procrustes alignment by stripping away language-specific anisotropy [Lim et al., 2025, Wendler et al., 2024] before alignment.

We originally set out to validate this hypothesis. Our experiments across 17 models spanning 5 architecture families and 4 cross-lingual pairs tell a different story. The causal geometry—specifically, the eigenvector directions of Σ\Sigma—does not measurably improve cross-lingual transport in our matched-spectrum test (Section 4). But the failure of the geometric hypothesis revealed something more interesting: activation-space concept representations systematically anti-concentrate in the eigenspectrum of Σ\Sigma, preferentially encoding in low-variance directions (Section 5). This phenomenon is not an artifact of the extraction method—it persists across sparse autoencoder features, linear probes, and difference-of-means vectors (Section 6). Moreover, the static vocabulary shows the opposite pattern: concept-specific unembedding-row differences concentrate in high-variance directions, revealing a dual geometry between the vocabulary space and the reasoning space (Section 7).

We provide functional evidence for why this dual geometry exists through two complementary experiments: steering experiments showing that injecting concept vectors along high-variance eigendirections causes significantly more perplexity degradation than injection along low-variance directions on Gemma and Llama (Section 8.1), and a POS-tag probing experiment showing that syntactic information is preferentially encoded in the high-variance subspace for most tested architectures (Section 8.2).

Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    A negative result for causal eigendirections in cross-lingual transport, established via matched-spectrum randomization across 17 models (Section 4).

  2. 2.

    The discovery and validation of spectral anti-concentration of activation-space concept representations, supported by three independent extraction methods across five architecture families (Sections 5 and 6).

  3. 3.

    The identification of a dual geometry between vocabulary-space concentration and activation-space anti-concentration, with a random-pair null model showing concept-specific structure (Section 7).

  4. 4.

    Functional evidence for why concepts anti-concentrate, via split-injection steering experiments across five models and syntactic probing of spectral subspaces across eight models (Sections 8.1 and 8.2).

All code and data are publicly available.11 1 https://github.com/pratyush-acharya/spectral_anti_concentration

2 Background

2.1 The Linear Representation Hypothesis

The idea that concepts are linearly encoded in neural network representations traces back to the word embedding literature [Mikolov et al., 2013a, Mikolov et al., 2013b]. Recent work has extended this to contextualized LLM representations, demonstrating linear encoding of truth [Marks and Tegmark, 2024, Burns et al., 2023], sentiment [Tigges et al., 2024], world state [Nanda et al., 2023], and refusal behavior [Arditi et al., 2024]. Park et al. [2024] provide the first rigorous formalization, defining linear representations via counterfactual pairs and proving connections between subspace representation, measurement (probing), and intervention (steering). Engels et al. [2025] show that some features are inherently multi-dimensional, suggesting the one-dimensional LRH is an approximation.

2.2 The Causal Inner Product

A key contribution of Park et al. [2024] is the identification of a non-Euclidean inner product under which causally separable concepts are orthogonal. Let WU∈ℝV×dW_{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d} be the unembedding matrix mapping from the dd-dimensional residual stream to VV-dimensional logits. The theoretical causal inner product is defined via the second moment of the unembedding vectors [Park et al., 2024].

In practice, we compute an empirical variant restricted to language-specific token subsets. Given a set of tokens ℒ\mathcal{L} belonging to a particular language (identified via Unicode script filtering), we define:

Σℒ=1|ℒ|​∑w∈ℒγ⁡(w)​γ​(w)⊤+λ​I\Sigma_{\mathcal{L}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{L}|}\sum_{w\in\mathcal{L}}\gamma(w)\gamma(w)^{\top}+\lambda I (1)

where γ⁡(w)∈ℝd\gamma(w)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the unembedding vector (row of WUW_{U}) for token ww and λ>0\lambda>0 is a regularization parameter.22 2 When ℒ\mathcal{L} is the full vocabulary and all tokens are weighted equally, this reduces to (1/V)​WU⊤​WU+λ​I(1/V)W_{U}^{\top}W_{U}+\lambda I, the form given by Park et al. [2024]. We compute this over language-specific subsets to isolate the geometry relevant to each language independently. The causal inner product is then ⟨u,v⟩C=u⊤​Σℒ−1​v\langle u,v\rangle_{C}=u^{\top}\Sigma_{\mathcal{L}}^{-1}v, under which causally separable concepts are orthogonal [Park et al., 2024]. The extension to categorical and hierarchical concepts is developed in Park et al. [2025].

2.3 Cross-Lingual Alignment and Whitened Causal Alignment

Cross-lingual transfer methods typically align representation spaces via orthogonal Procrustes analysis [Conneau et al., 2018], finding a rotation QQ minimizing ‖Xsrc−Xtgt​Q‖F\|X_{\text{src}}-X_{\text{tgt}}Q\|_{F} subject to Q⊤​Q=IQ^{\top}Q=I. However, Lim et al. [2025] show that language-specific latent processes hinder cross-lingual transfer, and Wendler et al. [2024] demonstrate that the “shared” semantic space in multilingual LLMs is predominantly English-centric.

Combining the causal inner product with Procrustes alignment yields Whitened Causal Alignment (wca). Given source and target covariances Σsrc\Sigma_{\text{src}} and Σtgt\Sigma_{\text{tgt}}, the wca transport of a concept vector vsrcv_{\text{src}} is:

vraid=Σtgt1/2Q⊤Σsrc−1/2vsrcv_{\text{raid}}=\Sigma_{\text{tgt}}^{1/2}\;Q^{\top}\;\Sigma_{\text{src}}^{-1/2}\;v_{\text{src}} (2)

where QQ is the Procrustes rotation solved in the whitened space. We evaluate transport quality via the cosine similarity between vraidv_{\text{raid}} and the ground-truth target concept vector vtgtv_{\text{tgt}}.

2.4 Anisotropy in Transformer Representations

Transformer representations are known to be highly anisotropic—activations cluster in a narrow cone of the full space [Ethayarajh, 2019, Gao et al., 2019]. This anisotropy is driven by a few “outlier” dimensions with disproportionately large variance, often linked to token frequency [Timkey and van Schijndel, 2021, Puccetti et al., 2022, Kovaleva et al., 2021]. Gurnee and Tegmark [2023] show that some of these high-variance dimensions encode spatial and temporal features, suggesting that the dominant eigenspace carries structured information rather than pure noise. The relationship between this anisotropy and the spectral structure of the unembedding covariance is central to our findings.

2.5 Sparse Autoencoders

Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose polysemantic neural activations into sparse, interpretable features [Bricken et al., 2023, Cunningham et al., 2024, Templeton et al., 2024]. The decoder column vectors of a trained SAE represent directions in activation space corresponding to individual learned features. Crucially, SAE features are extracted from contextualized residual stream activations via reconstruction loss—not contrastive subtraction—making them methodologically independent of difference-of-means concept extraction. We use open SAE suites including Gemma Scope [Lieberum et al., 2024] and Llama Scope [He et al., 2024].

3 Experimental Setup

3.1 Models

We evaluate 17 models across 5 architecture families (Table 1): Llama 3.2 (1B, 3B), Llama 3.1 (8B); Qwen 2.5 (0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, 14B); Qwen 3 (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, 8B); Gemma 2 (2B, 9B); Mistral 7B-v0.3; SmolLM2-1.7B; and two Mixture-of-Experts models (OLMoE-1B-7B, JetMoE-8B). Hidden dimensions range from 896 to 5120, and vocabulary sizes from 32K to 256K. Full details are in Appendix A.

3.2 Concepts

We extract 27 concept directions spanning four categories from the counterfactual word-pair dataset of Park et al. [2024], originally sourced from the Big Analogy Test Set [Gladkova et al., 2016]: Verb Morphology (10 concepts, e.g., [verb-Ved], [verb-Ving]), Semantic (7 concepts, e.g., [male-female], [country-capital]), Grammatical (6 concepts, combining adjective and noun morphology), and Language Pairs (4 concepts, e.g., [English-French]). Each concept is defined by 4–228 counterfactual word pairs.

3.3 Concept Extraction: Three Independent Methods

A central methodological concern is whether any single extraction method introduces spectral biases. We therefore employ three independent approaches, each operating on different inputs and using different algorithms:

Method 1: Difference-of-means on residual activations (subtractive).

For each concept, we compute the mean difference of pooled residual-stream activations from the final layer:

vdom=1N​∑i=1N(h⁡(wi+)−h⁡(wi−))v_{\text{dom}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(h(w_{i}^{+})-h(w_{i}^{-})\right) (3)

where h⁡(w)h(w) is the model’s pooled residual-stream representation for word ww when presented in isolation. This operates in activation space, not in the static unembedding matrix. As a subtractive method, it can mechanically cancel shared high-variance components between paired words, creating a potential artifact bias toward low-variance directions (see Section 6).

Method 2: Sparse autoencoder features (contextualized, unsupervised).

We use pre-trained SAEs from Gemma Scope [Lieberum et al., 2024] and Llama Scope [He et al., 2024] to extract concept directions from contextualized residual stream activations. For each concept, we pass word pairs through the model, record SAE feature activations, and select the top-kk most differentially activating features. The corresponding SAE decoder column vectors serve as concept directions. No subtraction is involved; features are learned via reconstruction loss on the full activation distribution.

Method 3: Linear probes (contextualized, supervised).

We train L2-regularized logistic regression classifiers on raw, uncentered contextualized activations at the final layer, predicting concept membership. The classifier weight vector defines the concept direction. L2 regularization biases the solution toward high-variance directions (opposing anti-concentration), making this a conservative test.

The convergence of all three methods—one activation-based/subtractive, one contextualized/unsupervised, one contextualized/supervised—is the core evidence for our claims.

3.4 Spectral Analysis Framework

All spectral analyses project concept vectors onto the eigenbasis of the language-specific unembedding covariance Σℒ\Sigma_{\mathcal{L}} (Equation 1).

Definition 1 (Spectral Energy Distribution).

Given a concept vector v∈ℝdv\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and the eigendecomposition Σ=U​Λ​U⊤\Sigma=U\Lambda U^{\top} with eigenvalues λ1≥⋯≥λd\lambda_{1}\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{d}, the fractional spectral energy at eigenvector uiu_{i} is Ei=(v⊤​ui)2/‖v‖2E_{i}=(v^{\top}u_{i})^{2}/\|v\|^{2}. The cumulative energy is C⁡(k)=∑i=1kEiC(k)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}E_{i}.

Definition 2 (Cumulative Variance).

V⁡(k)=∑i=1kλi/Tr⁡(Σ)V(k)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}/\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma). We plot C⁡(k)C(k) against V⁡(k)V(k)—not the raw index k/dk/d—to enable comparison across models with different hidden dimensions.

Definition 3 (Gini Deviation).

The signed area between the concept’s cumulative energy CDF (plotted against V⁡(k)V(k)) and the uniform baseline (y=xy=x). Negative values indicate anti-concentration (energy in the spectral tail); positive values indicate concentration (energy in top eigenvalues).

Definition 4 (Spectral Center of Mass).

The V⁡(k)V(k) value at which C⁡(k)C(k) reaches 50%. An scm near 1.0 means concepts encode primarily in low-eigenvalue directions.

For POS probing and split-injection experiments, we partition the eigenbasis at k=⌊0.1​d⌋k=\lfloor 0.1d\rfloor (top/bottom 10% of eigenvectors). We test robustness to this cutoff by repeating POS probing at k∈{5%,10%,20%}k\in\{5\%,10\%,20\%\}: the qualitative pattern (6/8 English models with positive gaps, 2 Qwen 2.5 models reversing) is invariant across all three cutoffs (Appendix H).

4 The Causal Geometry Does Not Aid Cross-Lingual Transport

To determine whether wca’s benefit stems from the specific geometric directions of Σ\Sigma or merely from its spectral shape, we construct matched-spectrum fake covariance matrices: Σfake=V​Λ​V⊤\Sigma_{\text{fake}}=V\Lambda V^{\top}, where Λ\Lambda contains the true eigenvalues and VV is a random orthogonal matrix (Haar-distributed via QR decomposition). We run the full wca pipeline with Σfake\Sigma_{\text{fake}} for both source and target, repeating with 5 random seeds across all 17 models ×\times 4 language pairs.

Across 68 model-pair combinations at λ=0.1\lambda=0.1: Real wca achieves a 50.3% win rate over Naive Procrustes (mean Δ=+0.0009\Delta=+0.0009), while Fake wca achieves 51.0% (Δ=+0.0010\Delta=+0.0010). The paired tt-test yields p=0.95p=0.95. We find no evidence that the specific eigenvector directions of Σ\Sigma contribute to cross-lingual transport beyond the matched eigenvalue spectrum. Within this experimental resolution, any benefit of wca appears attributable to spectral regularization—dampening high-variance directions regardless of their semantic content—rather than to semantically meaningful causal eigendirections.

5 Spectral Anti-Concentration of Concept Representations

Although the causal geometry failed to provide a measurable alignment advantage, the matched-spectrum experiment required computing eigendecompositions of Σ\Sigma for all 17 models, which naturally led us to examine how concept vectors distribute across these eigenbases. The result was a striking empirical regularity: activation-space concept vectors consistently place disproportionate energy in the low-variance tail of the eigenspectrum.

Across all 17 models, difference-of-means concept vectors show highly significant anti-concentration (mean Gini =−0.282=-0.282, all within-model p<10−6p<10^{-6}). The SCM gap between concept and random baselines is +0.169+0.169 on average, and crucially, this gap is independent of the background spectral shape (correlation between random scm and concept scm: r=0.019r=0.019, p=0.94p=0.94). Anti-concentration is not a ceiling effect driven by eigenvalue concentration at scale.

We tested whether different concept categories occupy different spectral bands. Pairwise Wilcoxon tests yielded no significant differences between most groups (e.g., Verb Morphology vs. Semantic: p=0.73p=0.73), with one exception (Grammatical vs. Language Pairs: p=0.006p=0.006). All concept types anti-concentrate to roughly the same degree.

6 Ruling Out the Subtraction Artifact

The difference-of-means method (Equation 3) mechanically cancels shared high-variance components between counterfactual pairs. If positive and negative tokens share a large projection onto the top eigenvectors of Σ\Sigma (as they should, being drawn from the same vocabulary), the subtraction eliminates high-eigenvalue energy by construction. We rule out this artifact using Methods 2 and 3 (Section 3.3).

6.1 SAE Feature Validation

We extract SAE-derived concept directions from Gemma Scope (gemma-2-2b, layer 20; gemma-2-9b, layer 31; width 16K) [Lieberum et al., 2024] and Llama Scope (Llama-3.1-8B, layer 24; width 32K) [He et al., 2024]. For each concept, we identify the top-kk most differentially activating features and use their decoder column vectors.

All SAE models show strong anti-concentration (Table 3). On gemma-2-2b, the top-5 averaged features yield stronger anti-concentration than top-1, ruling out the concern that feature collapse (where multiple concepts map to a single default SAE feature) drives the result.33 3 With top-1 selection, feature #11527 appeared for 5/27 concepts on gemma-2-2b. Its Gini (−0.147-0.147) was the weakest in the set; removing collapsed features strengthened the aggregate to −0.240-0.240. With top-5 selection, 84/135 feature slots were unique. See Appendix C for details.

6.2 Linear Probe Validation

L2-regularized logistic regression on uncentered activations achieves near-perfect accuracy on Llama-3.2-3B (mean >0.99>0.99, Gini =−0.167=-0.167, p<10−13p<10^{-13}) and Qwen2.5-3B (mean >0.99>0.99, Gini =−0.185=-0.185, p<10−15p<10^{-15}). Probes failed on gemma-2-9b (50% accuracy on 25/27 concepts), likely due to interaction between uncentered inputs and Gemma’s RMSNorm scaling; we exclude this model from probe-based claims.44 4 The gemma-2-9b probe failure illustrates a methodological limitation of uncentered probing, not evidence against anti-concentration. SAE validation on the same model (p=5.6×10−28p=5.6\times 10^{-28}) supports anti-concentration via a different method.

6.3 Synthesis

Three independent activation-space methods converge: anti-concentration is a robust property of these concept representations, not an artifact of difference-of-means subtraction alone.

7 The Dual Geometry

7.1 Unembedding Vectors Concentrate

We construct a separate set of concept directions directly from static unembedding rows: vunembed=meani​(γ⁡(wi+)−γ⁡(wi−))v_{\text{unembed}}=\text{mean}_{i}(\gamma(w_{i}^{+})-\gamma(w_{i}^{-})), restricted to word pairs where both tokens are single-token in the model’s vocabulary. Strikingly, these directions concentrate in the high-variance eigenspace (positive Gini), showing the opposite spectral tendency from activation-space concept representations.

7.2 Concept Pairs Are Anomalous

To determine whether this concentration is trivially expected, we compare against a null model of 1,000 random token-pair differences from the same vocabulary.

Random pairs mildly anti-concentrate (mean Gini ≈−0.10\approx-0.10), while concept pairs actively concentrate (mean Gini ≈+0.07\approx+0.07). The difference is significant across all four models (p<10−4p<10^{-4}; Table 4). The unembedding matrix specifically encodes concept-relevant contrasts along its principal axes.

7.3 Interpretation

The dual geometry can be summarized as:

  • •

    Vocabulary space: The unembedding matrix places concept contrasts along high-variance directions, where they maximally influence logit differences during token prediction.

  • •

    Reasoning space: Activation-space representations (difference-of-means vectors, SAE features, probe directions) encode concept information in the spectral tail, away from the dominant structural variance.

The transformer appears to perform a spectral rotation between these two regimes during forward processing, though the layer-wise timing of this rotation remains to be measured directly.

8 Why Concepts Anti-Concentrate

The dual geometry motivates a functional explanation. We provide two complementary experiments: a split-injection steering test measuring perplexity degradation as a proxy for grammatical interference, and a POS-tag probing experiment characterizing what the spectral subspaces encode.

8.1 Split-Injection: Interference Asymmetry

We decompose each concept vector into spectral components: projection onto the top-kk (“shouting”), middle, and bottom-kk (“whispering”) eigenvectors, where k=0.1​dk=0.1d. For each component, we steer the model at 4 layers (50%, 62%, 75%, 87% depth) with scaling factor α\alpha and measure perplexity on 10 held-out Wikipedia passages. We test five models spanning four architecture families.

Interference asymmetry is observed on three of five models (Tables 5, 8 and 9). We report α\alpha values in the informative range where PPL disruption is measurable but sub-catastrophic, acknowledging that this range is model-dependent and was selected after inspecting the full sweep (see Appendix F). On Gemma-2-2b, the shouting component causes 22–3×3\times more perplexity increase at α=10\alpha=10–2020 (Cohen’s d>0.8d>0.8). On Llama-3.1-8B, the effect is even stronger: at α=5\alpha=5, shouting produces +383%+383\% PPL increase vs. +223%+223\% for whispering (d=1.80d=1.80, p<10−4p<10^{-4}). On Llama-3.2-3B, the asymmetry is significant at low α\alpha (d=1.45d=1.45 at α=1\alpha=1) but washes out at higher steering strengths. On Qwen2.5-3B and Mistral-7B, no consistent shouting-greater-than-whispering asymmetry is observed; the whispering component causes equal or greater disruption than the shouting component.

8.2 POS-Tag Probing of Spectral Subspaces

The interference experiment suggests that high-variance injection can degrade fluency, but does not directly verify that syntactic information resides in those directions. We test this by training POS-tag classifiers on activations projected onto spectral subspaces.

We extract residual-stream activations from 500 sentences of Universal Dependencies English-EWT [Nivre et al., 2016] (6,585 tokens, 13 POS tags after filtering rare tags), project them onto the top-kk and bottom-kk eigenvectors of Σ\Sigma (k=0.1​dk=0.1d), and train 13-class logistic regression classifiers with 5-fold stratified cross-validation. We test 8 models spanning 5 architecture families.

Six of eight models show that the high-variance subspace carries significantly more POS information (Tables 6 and 10). The effect is strongest on the Llama family (+5.2+5.2 pp on Llama-3.2-3B, +1.6+1.6 pp on Llama-3.1-8B) and Gemma (+4.8+4.8 pp). The consistency of the direction (positive gap in 6/8 architectures) rather than the magnitude of individual gaps constitutes the primary evidence. The two Qwen 2.5 models (3B and 7B) are the only exceptions: the bottom-kk subspace carries slightly more POS information than top-kk, reversing the expected pattern.

Qwen 3 comparison.

Notably, Qwen 3-4B—which shares the same vocabulary (152K tokens) and a similar multilingual training distribution as Qwen 2.5—shows the expected positive gap (+1.8+1.8 pp, p=.001p=.001). This argues against a simple multilingual explanation.

Cross-lingual control.

To test whether the Qwen 2.5 reversal reflects a language mismatch (English-derived covariance applied to a Chinese-dominant model), we repeated the probing experiment on Qwen 2.5-3B and Qwen 3-4B using UD Chinese-GSD (10,813 tokens). Both models show a bottom-kk advantage on Chinese (Qwen 2.5-3B: −5.1-5.1 pp; Qwen 3-4B: −1.3-1.3 pp), indicating that language and corpus interact with the spectral allocation of POS information (see Appendix G for details).

In all cases, both subspaces substantially underperform the full-dimensional probe (78–86%), indicating that POS information is distributed across the full spectrum. The key finding is a measurable bias: on the majority of architectures, the high-variance subspace encodes more syntactic information, consistent with the interference asymmetry results of Section 8.1.

9 Discussion

Scaling behavior.

The Qwen 2.5 family (0.5B–14B) and Qwen 3 family (0.6B–8B) allow us to check whether anti-concentration changes with model capacity. The SCM gap remains positive at all tested scales (+0.205+0.205 to +0.286+0.286 for Qwen 2.5; +0.215+0.215 to +0.259+0.259 for Qwen 3), but does not follow a clear monotonic trend. We interpret this as evidence that anti-concentration is a robust property present at all tested scales, rather than a phenomenon that systematically deepens with capacity. Full scaling data are in Appendix D.

Architecture effects.

Gemma and Mistral models exhibit the highest condition numbers (1.6×1051.6\times 10^{5} to 2.8×1052.8\times 10^{5}) and most aggressive eigenvalue concentration, driven by their vocabulary characteristics. Despite this, both Gemma and Llama families show significant anti-concentration, and MoE models (OLMoE, JetMoE) exhibit similar patterns. This suggests that anti-concentration is not specific to dense FFNs versus sparse expert mixtures. See Appendix E for details.

Connection to superposition.

Elhage et al. [2022] demonstrate that neural networks represent more features than dimensions via superposition, exploiting feature sparsity. Our findings suggest a spectral dimension to this phenomenon. If the high-variance eigenspace is “claimed” by frequent, high-information syntactic patterns (articles, punctuation, positional structure), then the effective dimensionality available for semantic concept encoding is deff≪dd_{\text{eff}}\ll d. This forces the network into superposition for semantic features even when dd is large, because the usable subspace is restricted to the low-variance tail. Anti-concentration may thus be the spectral signature of how transformers allocate representational capacity: syntax gets the “loud” subspace where it can robustly survive the noise of the residual stream, while semantic concepts must share the “quiet” subspace via superposition [Elhage et al., 2022, Scherlis et al., 2022].

Implications for interpretability.

Methods that focus only on top principal components—such as PCA-based visualization or low-rank approximations—risk missing concept-level information. Our results suggest that interpretability tools should attend to the tail of the eigenspectrum. Conversely, Sharma et al. [2023] show that removing high-order SVD components (LASER) can improve reasoning, consistent with our finding that semantic content often appears in lower-variance directions.

Implications for steering.

The interference asymmetry (Section 8.1) suggests a practical refinement to activation engineering [Turner et al., 2024, Panickssery et al., 2024]: projecting steering vectors into the low-variance subspace before injection could achieve concept manipulation with lower fluency disruption. This may explain why naive steering often causes “aphasia”—the vector’s projection onto high-variance directions may disrupt syntactic routing [Arditi et al., 2024].

The Qwen 2.5 anomaly.

Both Qwen 2.5 models (3B, 7B) show reversed POS probing results and no interference asymmetry, while the closely related Qwen 3 (4B) shows the expected English POS gap. Chinese UD probing shows a bottom-kk advantage for both Qwen 2.5-3B and Qwen 3-4B, so the anomaly cannot be reduced to a single vocabulary-level explanation. A natural hypothesis is that Qwen 2.5’s relatively flat eigenspectrum (the lowest top-10% variance capture in our sample at 27%) makes the 10% cutoff insufficient to separate syntactic from semantic directions. However, our kk-sensitivity analysis (Appendix H) argues against this explanation: the Qwen 2.5 reversal persists at k=5%k=5\%, 10%10\%, and 20%20\%, while all six English confirming models maintain positive gaps across the same range. The anomaly is therefore likely architectural or training-dependent rather than an artifact of the spectral cutoff. This warrants further investigation into what specific aspects of Qwen 2.5’s training produce a different allocation of syntactic information across the eigenspectrum.

Limitations.

Our concepts are derived from word-level counterfactual pairs [Park et al., 2024, Gladkova et al., 2016], which capture morphological and simple semantic contrasts. Whether anti-concentration holds for more abstract concepts (e.g., honesty, sarcasm, planning) remains open. Additionally, our spectral analysis uses an uncentered, uniformly weighted unembedding second moment from a single matrix; centered, frequency-weighted, layer-wise, or activation-covariance spectra may reveal different structure. A layer-wise analysis of how anti-concentration develops through the transformer stack could reveal when the vocabulary-to-reasoning rotation occurs. Our split-injection experiments steer at 4 layers simultaneously (50%, 62%, 75%, 87% depth); per-layer interference profiles were not logged separately, so we cannot report whether the asymmetry peaks at a particular depth—this would be informative future work. The functional evidence (Section 8) is strongest on Gemma and Llama; the null results on Qwen 2.5 and Mistral suggest the spectral separation of syntax and semantics may be architecture-dependent. POS probing significance is based on 5 cross-validation folds plus token-level bootstrap intervals; future work should use sentence- or document-clustered resampling. All tested models are decoder-only; encoder or encoder-decoder architectures may behave differently.

10 Related Work

Spectral analysis of neural networks.

Martin and Mahoney [2021] and Martin and Mahoney [2019] use Random Matrix Theory to characterize weight matrix spectra, identifying heavy-tailed self-regularization. Martin et al. [2021] show that spectral metrics predict model quality without training data. Staats et al. [2024] demonstrate that small singular values carry significant information in transformers, consistent with our finding that concepts reside in this regime.

Representation geometry.

Papyan et al. [2020] identify Neural Collapse in classification networks. Wu and Papyan [2024] explore analogous phenomena in language models. Our anti-concentration finding is conceptually distinct: rather than class means collapsing toward specific vertices, concepts are pushed away from the dominant spectral subspace.

Whitening in NLP.

Su et al. [2021] and Huang et al. [2021] show that whitening improves sentence embedding quality by counteracting anisotropy. Our results suggest a possible mechanistic explanation: whitening amplifies low-variance directions where many of our measured concept directions reside.

Steering and representation engineering.

Turner et al. [2024], Panickssery et al. [2024], Zou et al. [2023], and Li et al. [2024] develop methods for steering LLM behavior via activation addition. Subramani et al. [2022] extract latent steering vectors. Our split-injection results suggest that effective steering implicitly targets the spectral tail.

11 Conclusion

We set out to test whether the causal inner product provides a geometrically meaningful basis for cross-lingual concept transport. In our experiments, matched-spectrum randomization finds no advantage for the real causal eigendirections over randomized eigendirections with the same spectrum, suggesting that Whitened Causal Alignment acts primarily as spectral regularization. But the failure revealed a broader pattern in how transformers organize information.

Word-level concept directions—as measured by sparse autoencoder features, linear probes, and difference-of-means vectors across 17 models and 5 architecture families—systematically avoid the high-variance eigendirections of the unembedding covariance. They place disproportionate energy in the spectral tail, where our split-injection experiments on Gemma and Llama show reduced perplexity disruption relative to high-variance injection. POS-tag probing across 8 models shows that the high-variance subspace preferentially encodes syntactic information in 6 of 8 architectures. The static vocabulary shows the opposite pattern, placing concept contrasts along principal axes for maximal influence on token prediction.

This dual geometry—concepts whisper while syntax shouts—has immediate practical implications for how we probe, interpret, and steer large language models.

Appendix A Full Model Details

All models are decoder-only transformers using pre-normalization (RMSNorm for Gemma, Llama, Qwen, and Mistral; LayerNorm for SmolLM2 and the MoE models). Concept vectors and covariance matrices are computed from the unembedding matrix WUW_{U} accessed via each model’s language model head. For models that tie input embeddings and unembedding weights (Qwen, SmolLM2), WUW_{U} is the shared embedding matrix. Condition numbers span two orders of magnitude (2.6×1032.6\times 10^{3} to 2.8×1052.8\times 10^{5}), driven primarily by vocabulary size: Mistral’s 32K and Gemma’s 256K vocabularies produce the highest condition numbers among the tested models. All experiments use the base (non-instruct) model variants.

Appendix B Full Spectral Metrics (All 17 Models)

Several patterns are notable. First, all 17 models show negative Gini deviation, supporting broad anti-concentration across the tested set. Second, the Llama 3.2 family shows the smallest scm gaps (−0.010-0.010 to +0.001+0.001), meaning Llama concept vectors are more evenly distributed across the spectrum than other families, though they still anti-concentrate (negative Gini). Third, SmolLM2-1.7B shows the strongest Gini (−0.436-0.436) despite moderate size, suggesting that anti-concentration strength is not simply a function of model capacity. Fourth, OLMoE-1B-7B is the only model with a negative scm gap (−0.116-0.116), indicating its concept vectors are more uniformly distributed than random, though still anti-concentrated (Gini =−0.076=-0.076). The correlation between random scm and concept scm is negligible (r=0.019r=0.019, p=0.94p=0.94), suggesting that the anti-concentration gap is not simply determined by the background spectral shape.

Appendix C SAE Feature Collapse Analysis

On gemma-2-2b with top-1 selection, 21/27 concepts mapped to unique SAE features (77.8% unique). Three features appeared more than once: feature #11527 (5 concepts), #38 (2 concepts), and #1643 (2 concepts). Feature #11527 had the weakest Gini deviation (−0.147-0.147); removing the 5 collapsed concepts strengthened the mean Gini from −0.230-0.230 to −0.240-0.240.

With top-5 selection, 84/135 feature slots were unique. The aggregate Gini (−0.240-0.240, p=1.2×10−27p=1.2\times 10^{-27}) is stronger than top-1, confirming that collapse does not drive the result.

On gemma-2-9b with top-3, all 27 concepts mapped to distinct feature sets with zero collapse.

Appendix D Scaling Data

The Qwen 2.5 family shows a mild decrease in the scm gap from 0.5B (+0.286+0.286) to 14B (+0.205+0.205), but the trend is non-monotonic (the 7B model has gap +0.242+0.242, higher than the 3B at +0.238+0.238). Qwen 3 similarly shows no clear monotonic pattern. In both families, the Gini gap between concept and random vectors deepens with scale for the larger models, but the smallest models are outliers. We interpret this as evidence that anti-concentration is present at all tested scales rather than a phenomenon that emerges or disappears with capacity.

Appendix E Architecture Comparison

Gemma models exhibit the highest eigenvalue concentration (top 10% captures 40–52% of variance vs. 30–32% for Llama), consistent with their larger vocabulary (256K vs. 128K). Despite this structural difference, both families show strong anti-concentration. MoE models (OLMoE, JetMoE) exhibit similar patterns to dense models, suggesting that the phenomenon is not specific to whether computation is routed through dense FFNs or sparse expert mixtures.

Appendix F Split-Injection Details

The split-injection experiment steers at 4 layers (50%, 62%, 75%, 87% depth) using concept vectors from the difference-of-means extraction on the English en-fr covariance. Several concepts on gemma-2-2b show zero spectral energy (energy distribution: 0%/0%/0%) and produce no effect at any α\alpha; these correspond to concepts whose word pairs are multi-token for Gemma’s tokenizer, yielding zero-norm activation-derived vectors. These are excluded from the aggregate statistics reported in Section 8.1. Effective sample sizes: Neff=18N_{\text{eff}}=18 on gemma-2-2b (9 zero-energy concepts), N=27N=27 on all other models.

Table 10 reports the full summary across all five tested models and all steering strengths.

Appendix G POS Probing Details

POS-tag probes use 5-fold stratified cross-validation with L2-regularized logistic regression (C=1.0C=1.0, max_iter = 2000) on activations from the final hidden layer (after final norm). Significance is assessed via both paired tt-test on fold accuracies (N=5N=5) and bootstrap confidence interval on per-token accuracy differences (N=10,000N=10{,}000 resamples). Because folds are few and token-level bootstrap samples are not independent at the sentence level, the pp-values should be interpreted as descriptive evidence for a consistent direction rather than as definitive population-level inference. The corpus is UD English-EWT dev set (2,001 sentences, 25,147 tokens), filtered to tags with ≥30\geq 30 samples (13 tags, 6,585 tokens).

Table 11 reports the full per-model results including the variance captured by each subspace and the random-kk baseline accuracy.

Notably, the top-kk subspace captures 27–40% of total variance across models (far more than the k/d=10%k/d=10\% of dimensions would suggest under a uniform spectrum), while the bottom-kk captures only 1.5–2.6%. Despite this massive asymmetry in variance, the POS accuracy gap between subspaces is modest (1.4–5.2 pp for positive-gap models), indicating that syntactic information is encoded somewhat diffusely but with a measurable bias toward the high-variance subspace.

Chinese UD control.

For the Chinese UD control experiment, we use UD Chinese-GSD dev set (500 sentences, 10,813 tokens after filtering). Table 12 reports the results.

Appendix H POS Probing Sensitivity Analysis

To verify that our results are not artifacts of the k=10%k=10\% spectral cutoff, we repeated the POS-tag probing experiment (Section 8.2) using k∈{5%,10%,20%}k\in\{5\%,10\%,20\%\}.

Table 13 reports the top-kk and bottom-kk accuracies, the resulting gap, and statistical significance across all 8 models for each cutoff. The qualitative direction of the gap remains invariant across the entire range: all six English confirming models (Gemma, Llama, Mistral, SmolLM, Qwen 3) show a positive gap (Top-k>k> Bottom-kk), while both Qwen 2.5 models consistently show a negative gap. While k=10%k=10\% provides the cleanest statistical significance across the board (all 8 models significant at α=0.05\alpha=0.05), the magnitude and statistical power shrink predictably at extreme cutoffs because the subspaces become too small (5%5\%) or too noisy (20%20\%). Nonetheless, the directional invariance indicates that the English POS pattern is robust to the choice of kk. The persistence of the Qwen 2.5 reversal at k=20%k=20\% argues against the hypothesis that its flatter eigenspectrum simply required a larger subspace to capture syntactic information.
